comments.text:
I appreciate a lot of your insights and formulations, Wes. In particular what you said about people trying to reduce AI to a logic-based script/algorithm. People get emotional about it too, I guess it feels threatening to "human intelligence" in some way. In my opininon, people really need to start viewing upcoming A(G)I, as elevating both humans and machines, rather than reducing humans. We can learn so much. It is an intellectual synergy.

The other "reductionist" stab they'll throw is saying it cannot be conscious because it is merely "electrical signals", as if brain neurons differ from that. Every time you keep asking those people for more concrete distinctions, they keep moving the goalpost. "Okay, neurons are also electrical signals, but they can change". "Okay, the code might also be adaptive, but.."

Always trying to look for arbitrary differences without any real inherent ones. Slowly this is requiring more input from psychology and philosophy, the basid of AI might be IT tech, but the ways to understand it require much broader fields.

comments.author: @user-ei2kk2oh5v
comments.text: Sorry but I revoked my thumbsup, reason because I got tired of listening to this analogy with AlphaGo. I know that DeepMind, and even more so Nature, does the same in their presentation on their homepages, but your vid. seems to spend 50% on this analogy, then 25% on speculations about what type of impact AI/AGI will have on our society, and then basically nothing on in what sense this speedup is a speedup. For example, is it an Ordo-improvement, like in the P vs NP-problem; sorting is btw in P if we measure #steps required for a list with n elements since the naive way does it in O(n^2) steps. But just because an algo is fast in the strict Ordo-sense does not mean that it is fast in a practical sense; it might be that the improvement starts to kick in first for extremely large n (there might be an extremely large constant hidden in the Ordo-sign). On the other hand, a much used sorting-algo, Quicksort, does it in on average O(n*log n) steps, but if you're unlucky it can take O(n^2) steps. So I suspect that the algo that AlphaDev found might not be faster than the best known in this strict computer-science sense, but more in a sense that is actually useful in practice. Like Quicksort, it is not O(n*log n) because of these special cases, but is still in use because it is fast for practical purposes. In any case, it is of course up to you how you make your vids, and I enjoy them. But if it becomes too much of an overview, with analogies to make everybody kind of understand, then I'm not that interested. On the other hand, I am probably not your target audience, so in that case just keep up the good work!
